persons.name: Hiram Z. Britain
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Britain, Hiram Z. 2' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). persons.name: Ebenezer Goodrich
persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835, poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 4 March 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “GOODRICH EBENEZER”, 1833-10-22: 1 parcel of the school section — lot 1 of block 93 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $100.00 (ls0168). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: GOODRICH EBENEZER matches Ebenezer Goodrich: the forename names Ebenezer Goodrich of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Goodrich, Ebenezer” (poll_1834_045, line 214). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Goodrich' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - first of 1 tavern keeper households in this layer, in the north division. Seven tavern and hotel keepers are documented and the schedule allows ten inn or tavern roofs. One further keeper is inferred, for the single anonymous T1 roof the North Division parcel placed - a small inn on the north side, which the documented layer does not reach. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one. RETIRED AN INVENTED NAME (T-0264). This household was raised by the occupation census and named from the invented-name pools. The newspaper register matched it to J. Shrigley, a documented tavern keeper the corpus names 1 time(s) and places nowhere in particular, and he now holds the roof. What changed is WHO: the argument for the household, its dwelling and its position are untouched and still the reconstruction's, and the person's grade is `inferred` — a real man with reconstructed details — rather than `attested`, which would claim the dwelling too. tools/replace_invented_residents.py derives this deal and prints every candidate it refused. T-0489: reconstructed occupancy retired; evidence-based person retained and unplaced.

persons.name: Ashbel Steele
persons.note: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'. It gives a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, and it is a retrospective of 1884: a YEAR off it is documented, a MONTH is not, and it says nothing whatever about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Steele, Ashbel” (poll_1834_104, line 273); Poll list of 1835 — “Steele, Ashbel” (poll_1835_076, line 363). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Steele' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “Ashbel Steele” as sheriff of cook county, 1840 (f1839_r0092, printed page 39). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Steele' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins A. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 3 times, as “STEELE ASHBEL”, 1833-10-22: 3 parcels of the school section — BL4 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 2 of block 26 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 7 of block 26 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 3.69 acres stated in all, for $173.00 (ls0340, ls0341, ls0342). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: STEELE ASHBEL matches Ashbel Steele: the forename names Ashbel Steele of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: THE ONLY PLASTERER IN THE DATASET, AND THE ONLY MAN IN IT DOCUMENTED BY A SINGLE JOB. What makes him worth a record is what the job proves about a building: the town's ordinances of 7 November 1833 legislate for 'wooden buildings with wooden and lath-and-plaster partitions', and this is a named man doing exactly that work in the same month, in a building this dataset models. THE LINK IS NOT MADE IN works_at because plastering a room once is not working somewhere; it is recorded here.
